# Detienne & Vernant — Cunning Intelligence in Greek Culture and Society (1978)

## Bibliographic identity

The target work is Marcel Detienne and Jean-Pierre Vernant, *Cunning Intelligence in Greek Culture and Society*, translated by Janet Lloyd (Hassocks: Harvester Press, 1978), the English rendering of *Les ruses de l'intelligence: la métis des Grecs* (Paris: Flammarion, 1974). The Lloyd translation was reissued in paperback by the University of Chicago Press in 1991; the two printings are believed to share pagination, but this has not been confirmed, and the consulted edition must be pinned when a physical or fully readable copy is acquired. All page references in this house (pp. 3, 13, 272–73, and the ch. 10 span 269–75) currently follow the 1978 Harvester printing as cited in the verifying secondary literature.

## Source scholarship

Detienne and Vernant reconstruct *mētis* — cunning, resourceful, polymorphic intelligence — as a coherent category of Greek thought that the Greeks themselves never theorised in a treatise, and that philosophy after Plato actively occluded. Their method is to read the category out of its scattered operations: hunting and trapping, fishing, weaving and net-making, navigation and the pilot's art, medicine, rhetoric, the charioteer's turn, and the craftsman's work. What emerges is not a loose family resemblance but, in their words, a "complex but very coherent body of mental attitudes and intellectual behavior" (p. 3): an intelligence that operates in shifting, ambiguous situations, that binds itself to the fluid and polymorphic in order to master it, and whose instruments — the trap, the net, the woven circle, the bond — reproduce its own suppleness in material form.

The book's structural logic is exactly the logic of the Odyssey 8 gnome (lame Hephaestus catches the swiftest of the gods, 8.329–32). The signature of *mētis*, Detienne and Vernant argue, is to "revers[e] the 'natural' outcome of the encounter," because "whatever the strength of god or man, there always comes a time when he confronts one stronger than himself" (p. 13): force meets its ceiling; cunning has none, since it wins precisely where it is weaker. Hephaestus is one of their canonical carriers of this reversal. His crooked feet are "the visible symbol" of "his metis, his wise thoughts and his craftsman's intelligence" (p. 272) — the deformity is not the negation of his power but its emblem, a "double and divergent orientation" that lets him "dominate shifting, fluid powers" (p. 273), the walking-both-ways of an intelligence at home in ambiguity.

Chapter 10, "The Circle and the Bond," is the chapter most directly on-point for the essay and the one passage-block still awaiting extraction. There the circle, the net, and the *desmos* are treated as the canonical instruments of *mētis*: the bond is the woven circle that closes around a polymorphic victim, defeating shape-shifting by enclosing every shape at once — the victim cannot out-turn what has no open direction. This is the precise scholarly frame for Hephaestus's δεσμοὶ τεχνήεντες: bonds finer than spider-silk, invisible even to the gods, encircling the bed itself. The chapter's exact sentences on the Ares–Aphrodite bonds have been located to the chapter span (pp. 269–75) but not yet transcribed; the accessible scan is not machine-readable, and quotation waits on the print edition.

The book's authority for the essay is that of a foundational structuralist study: it established *mētis* as a live scholarly category, and subsequent classical scholarship on trickery, craft, and binding routinely routes through it. The three verified quotations above were collated not from the book directly but from a scholarly article quoting the 1978 Lloyd translation — Jay Dolmage, "'Breathe Upon Us an Even Flame': Hephaestus, History, and the Body of Rhetoric," *Rhetoric Review* 25, no. 2 (2006) — which is a lawful but second-hand verification channel; the wording is treated as reliable, the print collation as still owed.

## Essay use

### Source's relevant contribution

Detienne and Vernant supply the scholarly control establishing that the bond, the net, and the reversal of strength by craft are not incidental furniture of the Demodocus song but instruments and logic of a coherent Greek category of intelligence — and that Hephaestus is that category's divine craftsman-bearer.

### Licensed essay use

- Establish *mētis* as a coherent Greek craft-intelligence category with the bond and net among its canonical instruments (q001, q004).
- Ground the essay's reading of the lame-catches-swift gnome (Od. 8.329–32) in the reversal-logic of *mētis* (q002).
- Ground the reading of Hephaestus's lameness as the emblem of his craft-intelligence rather than a mere defect (q003).
- Serve the myth history and the ancient-philosophy history as the standard scholarly reconstruction of the category.

### Claim boundary

Detienne and Vernant establish *mētis* and the bond as a Greek craft-intelligence category; they do not connect the Ares–Aphrodite episode to modern technology, surveillance, enframing, or Heidegger. Every step from their category to the essay's technological reading — σκοπιή as surveillance, the *desmos* as capture-apparatus, the staged ἴδησθε as evidence-production — is the essay's own Argued or Offered development and may not be attributed to this source.
